title: The Integumentary System
subtitle: Your largest organ is the one you're wearing.
objectives: Name the three layers of skin and what each one does
Explain how skin regulates body temperature
Describe the roles of sweat glands, oil glands and hair
Explain what melanin does and why it matters
Relate skin changes at puberty to hormone activity

cards.title: Your biggest organ isn't inside you
cards.text: Skin covers about two square metres and makes up roughly a sixth of your body weight. It is an organ, and it is doing several jobs right now.

cards.title: Five jobs, one surface
cards.text: Like the skeleton, skin gets thought of as one thing. It's doing five.
points: **Barrier** — keeps water and heat in, germs out.
**Temperature control** — sweating and blood flow.
**Sensation** — touch, pressure, pain, temperature.
**Vitamin D** — your skin makes it from sunlight.

cards.title: Tap any layer or structure
cards.text: Three layers plus the things buried in them. Two quiz questions come from this diagram.

cards.title: Epidermis — the part you can see
cards.text: The outer layer, and its surface cells are already dead. You are wearing a coat of your own dead cells right now.
points: **No blood vessels at all.** It's fed from below.
**New cells push up from underneath** and flatten as they go.
**Fully replaced about every four weeks.**

cards.title: It's paint, primer and padding
cards.text: Car bodywork is layered for exactly the same reason skin is: different jobs need different materials.
points: **Epidermis** = clear coat. Thin, sacrificial, replaced not repaired.
**Dermis** = the panel with the wiring behind it.
**Subcutaneous fat** = the padding that absorbs a knock.

cards.title: Cyberpunk's subdermal armour is in the right layer
cards.text: The game installs armour *under* the skin, not on top of it. Whoever designed that knew the anatomy.
points: **Sub-dermal means below the dermis.** That's the padding layer.
**It's exactly where your own cushioning sits.**
**You already have version one installed.**

question.text: Which skin layer has no blood vessels in it?
question.explain: The epidermis. It's fed by the dermis below, which is why a shallow scrape doesn't bleed.

cards.title: Dermis — where everything actually happens
cards.text: The thick working layer. Blood vessels, nerve endings, sweat glands, oil glands and hair roots all live here.
points: **Every touch you feel** starts with a nerve ending in here.
**Collagen fibres** make it tough and stretchy.
**Cut this deep and you bleed**, because this is where the vessels are.

cards.title: Subcutaneous — the padding
cards.text: Fat and connective tissue underneath. It insulates you, stores energy, and cushions impact.
points: **Insulation.** Fat is a poor conductor of heat, which is useful.
**Shock absorption.** It spreads a blow before it reaches anything solid.
**Energy store** your body draws on between meals.

question.text: Put the skin layers in order, from outside to inside.
question.explain: Outside in: epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous. Epi- means 'upon', so the epidermis sits upon the dermis.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Layers done. Part 2 is cooling, pigment and what puberty is doing to your skin. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Your skin is your radiator
cards.text: Your body has to stay near 37 °C. Too far either way and things stop working. Skin is how it holds the line.

cards.title: Sweating, and why it only works if it evaporates
cards.text: Sweat doesn't cool you by being wet. It cools you when it turns to vapour and carries heat away.
points: **Two to four million sweat glands** across your body.
**Evaporation is the cooling.** Wiping sweat off cancels it.
**Blood vessels widen too**, dumping heat through the skin.

cards.title: Trained people sweat sooner
cards.text: This surprises people. Fitness doesn't stop you sweating — it makes you start earlier.
points: **Your body learns to cool before it overheats**, not after.
**That's an adaptation**, the same as bone getting denser.
**Humid air blocks evaporation**, which is why it feels far worse.

question.text: Sweat cools you down by evaporating, not simply by being wet on your skin.
question.explain: True. Turning from liquid to vapour takes energy, and it takes that heat from you. Wiping it off throws away the cooling.

cards.title: Melanin is sun armour
cards.text: Melanocytes in the epidermis make melanin. It absorbs ultraviolet light before it can damage the DNA in your cells.
points: **Everyone has roughly the same number** of melanocytes.
**Skin colour comes from how much melanin they make.**
**A tan is a damage response**, not a sign of health.

cards.title: Goosebumps are Week 1 coming back
cards.text: Each hair grows from a follicle in the dermis, and a tiny muscle can pull it upright.
points: **That muscle is called arrector pili.**
**It's smooth muscle** — involuntary, from Week 1.
**In furrier animals it traps warm air.** On you it does almost nothing.

options: Absorbs ultraviolet light before it damages DNA
Helps the skin sweat more easily
question.explain: It's protection from UV. Sebum from oil glands is what waterproofs skin — different job entirely.

cards.title: Why puberty changes your skin
cards.text: Hormone levels rise and your oil glands respond by producing far more sebum than before.
points: **Sebum plus dead skin cells** can block a follicle.
**A blocked follicle is a spot.** That's the whole mechanism.
**It's hormones, not hygiene.** Scrubbing harder makes it worse.
**Sweat glands ramp up too**, which is where body odour starts.

cards.text: Most household dust is dead skin cells. You shed around 30,000 to 40,000 of them every minute.

terms.def: Skin, hair and nails — your body's outer covering.
The outer layer of skin. No blood vessels.
The thick layer below, holding vessels, nerves and glands.
Fat and connective tissue under the dermis. Also called hypodermis.
The pigment that absorbs ultraviolet light.
Oil that waterproofs skin and hair.
The pocket in the skin that a hair grows from.
The small muscle that stands a hair up. Goosebumps.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Three layers:** epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous — outside in.
**The epidermis has no blood vessels;** the dermis holds everything.
**Sweat cools by evaporating**, not by being wet.
**Melanin blocks UV.** Sebum waterproofs. Different jobs.

quiz.text: Put the layers of skin in order, from the outside inwards.
quiz.explain: Epi- means 'upon'. The epidermis sits upon the dermis, and the subcutaneous layer is under both.
quiz.objective: Name the three layers of skin and what each one does

quiz.text: Which layer contains the blood vessels, nerves and glands?
quiz.explain: The dermis is the working layer. The epidermis above it has no blood supply of its own.
quiz.objective: Name the three layers of skin and what each one does

quiz.text: The outermost cells of your epidermis are dead.
quiz.explain: True. New cells push up from below, flatten and die, forming a tough barrier before flaking away.
quiz.objective: Name the three layers of skin and what each one does

quiz.text: How does sweating cool you down?
options: Evaporating sweat carries heat away from the skin
Wet skin is naturally colder than dry skin
Sweat blocks heat from reaching the body
quiz.explain: Evaporation is the cooling step. That's why humid weather feels so much worse — sweat can't evaporate.
quiz.objective: Explain how skin regulates body temperature

quiz.text: What is the name of the pigment that protects your skin from ultraviolet light?
quiz.explain: Melanin, made by melanocytes in the epidermis. It absorbs UV before it can damage DNA.
quiz.objective: Explain what melanin does and why it matters

options: Hormones make oil glands produce more sebum, which blocks follicles
Not washing your face often enough
Sweat glands becoming blocked with salt
quiz.explain: It's hormonal. Extra sebum plus dead skin cells blocks a follicle. Scrubbing harder irritates skin and makes it worse.
quiz.objective: Relate skin changes at puberty to hormone activity

options: Waterproofs skin and hair and keeps them flexible
quiz.explain: Sebum is the waterproofing oil. Melanin is the UV blocker — a common mix-up in exams.
quiz.objective: Describe the roles of sweat glands, oil glands and hair

quiz.text: What kind of muscle makes your hair stand up in goosebumps?
quiz.explain: Smooth muscle — the involuntary type from Week 1. The muscle is called arrector pili.
quiz.objective: Describe the roles of sweat glands, oil glands and hair

quiz.text: People with darker skin have many more melanocytes than people with lighter skin.
quiz.explain: False. Almost everyone has a similar number of melanocytes. What differs is how much melanin those cells produce.
quiz.objective: Explain what melanin does and why it matters

quiz.text: Which job does the subcutaneous layer do?
options: Insulates, stores energy and cushions impact
quiz.explain: It's the padding. Fat insulates, stores energy, and spreads a blow before it reaches anything solid.
quiz.objective: Name the three layers of skin and what each one does

quiz.text: Someone who trains regularly starts sweating sooner than someone who doesn't.
quiz.explain: True. The body adapts to cool before it overheats rather than after. It's the same principle as bone getting denser.
quiz.objective: Explain how skin regulates body temperature

quiz.text: Your skin makes one vitamin using sunlight. Which one?
quiz.explain: Vitamin D, and it matters for this course — your body needs it to absorb the calcium that builds bone.
quiz.objective: Name the three layers of skin and what each one does

teacher.summary: Week 3 Science covers the integumentary system, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. It reuses the tappable-diagram interaction from Weeks 1 and 2, and deliberately connects back to both: goosebumps are smooth muscle from Week 1, and vitamin D links to the calcium absorption covered in Week 2. The puberty section treats acne mechanically rather than as a hygiene failing, which is both accurate and kinder to a Grade 6 reader living through it.
discussion: Ask why a shallow graze stings but does not bleed. The answer — no blood vessels in the epidermis — shows he has the layer structure.
Ask why a hot humid day feels worse than a hot dry one at the same temperature. It tests whether he understood that evaporation is the cooling step.
Ask what melanin and sebum each do. These two are the most commonly swapped answers on this topic.
Ask what goosebumps have to do with Week 1. Smooth muscle turning up in an unexpected place is worth noticing.
teacher.extension: Have him label a cross-section of skin from memory, then add one arrow showing where heat leaves the body and one showing where a hair grows from. Five minutes, and it tests structure and function together.
misconceptions: 'Acne is caused by being dirty.' It is caused by hormones increasing sebum production. Over-washing irritates skin and can worsen it.
'A tan is healthy.' A tan is the skin's response to UV damage that has already occurred.
'Sweat cools you because it is wet.' It cools you as it evaporates. Wiping it away removes the cooling.
'Skin is just a covering.' It is the body's largest organ and regulates temperature, senses the world, and manufactures vitamin D.
